title: Python: ownership and concurrency
summary: Twelve deeper exercises in resource ownership, reference lifetimes, context propagation, cancellation, bounded work and asynchronous shutdown. Use real Python objects and tasks.

lessons.title: Unwind partially acquired resources
lessons.body:
# Unwind partially acquired resources

Acquiring several resources is a transaction of its own. If the third acquisition fails, the first two still need cleanup, in reverse order. An ExitStack records ownership as each acquisition succeeds. Registering cleanup only after every acquisition works leaves a leak on the failure path.

This exercise accepts context-manager factories so the tests can fail a specific acquisition without files or network access. The same ownership pattern applies to files, temporary directories and database sessions. A context manager should return a resource only after it owns the cleanup obligation.

```python
from contextlib import ExitStack
log = []
with ExitStack() as stack:
    stack.callback(log.append, "first")
    stack.callback(log.append, "last")
print(log)
```

## Review the design

ExitStack unwinds successful entries in reverse order on every exit. It cannot clean up an acquisition that leaked before its own context manager registered ownership; that manager must implement its own partial-failure handling.
lessons.task: Implement acquire_all(factories, use). Enter each context manager in order, call use(resources) once, return its result and close everything in reverse order even if acquisition or use raises.

checks.name: successful reverse cleanup
checks.code:
from contextlib import contextmanager
log=[]
@contextmanager
def item(n):
 log.append(n); yield n; log.append(-n)
assert acquire_all([lambda:item(1),lambda:item(2)],sum)==3
assert log==[1,2,-2,-1]

checks.name: failed acquisition closes earlier resources
use failure propagates

hints: Register each resource through enter_context as soon as it opens.
Keep the use call inside the ExitStack scope.

ExitStack unwinds successful entries in reverse order on every exit. It cannot clean up an acquisition that leaked before its own context manager registered ownership; that manager must implement its own partial-failure handling.
lessons.explanation: ExitStack unwinds successful entries in reverse order on every exit. It cannot clean up an acquisition that leaked before its own context manager registered ownership; that manager must implement its own partial-failure handling.

lessons.title: Cache without owning object lifetimes
lessons.body:
# Cache without owning object lifetimes

A cache normally holds strong references, extending the lifetime of every value it stores. That can accidentally turn a memory optimization into unbounded retention. A WeakValueDictionary permits reuse while a caller still owns the object, but does not keep an otherwise unused object alive.

Weak references are not a replacement for resource cleanup or a bounded LRU cache. Not every Python value supports them, and an entry can disappear between accesses. Keep a strong local reference while returning a value. This exercise uses user-defined objects and explicit collection instead of relying on CPython reference-count timing.

```python
import weakref, gc
class Item: pass
value = Item()
cache = weakref.WeakValueDictionary()
cache["x"] = value
del value
gc.collect()
print(list(cache))
```

## Review the design

A weak cache delegates lifetime to callers. Losing an entry is normal behavior, so factory calls must be safe to repeat. Resource release still belongs in explicit context management, not in a finalizer.
lessons.task: Implement weak_cache(factory) returning get(key). Reuse a live value for that key without retaining it after all callers drop it. Values support weak references.

checks.name: live values are reused
checks.code:
class Item: pass
get=weak_cache(lambda k:Item()); a=get('x'); assert get('x') is a

checks.name: collection permits reconstruction
checks.code:
import weakref,gc
class Item: pass
made=[]
def create(k):
 made.append(k);return Item()
get=weak_cache(create);a=get('x');ref=weakref.ref(a);del a;gc.collect()
assert ref() is None
b=get('x');assert made==['x','x']

checks.name: keys stay independent
checks.code:

get=weak_cache(lambda k:Item());a=get('a');b=get('b');assert a is not b

lessons.title: Release resources when iteration stops early
lessons.body:
# Release resources when iteration stops early

A generator can suspend while a resource is open. Exhausting the iterator normally runs its finally block, but a consumer that takes one value and retains the generator can keep the resource alive. The consumer must close an owned iterator when it stops early.

This is observable behavior, not just a garbage-collection detail. Tests supply a generator with a finally log and verify cleanup before the consuming function returns. The boundary must also behave when the requested count is zero or the iterator raises during iteration. Cleanup belongs in finally rather than after a successful loop.

```python
def values(log):
    try: yield 1
    finally: log.append("closed")
log=[]
it=values(log)
print(next(it))
it.close()
print(log)
```

## Review the design

Closing a generator executes its finally block once it has started. An unstarted generator has not entered its resource-owning body, so closing it cannot run cleanup that was never acquired.
lessons.task: Implement take_owned(iterator,n) returning up to n values and always calling its close method if present. Reject negative n, including before iteration, while still closing the owned iterator.

checks.name: closes a partially consumed generator
checks.code:
log=[]
def gen():
 try:yield 1;yield 2
 finally:log.append('closed')
assert take_owned(gen(),1)==[1];assert log==['closed']

checks.name: exhaustion and plain iterators
checks.code:
assert take_owned(iter([1,2]),5)==[1,2]
assert take_owned(iter([1]),0)==[]

checks.name: negative counts still release ownership

hints: Drive next explicitly so no extra item is consumed.
Put validation and iteration inside a try with close in finally.

lessons.explanation: Closing a generator executes its finally block once it has started. An unstarted generator has not entered its resource-owning body, so closing it cannot run cleanup that was never acquired.

lessons.title: Restore request context after failures
lessons.body:
# Restore request context after failures

Request-local state must not become process-global state. ContextVar values follow an asynchronous context, while a module global is shared by unrelated requests. Setting a ContextVar returns a token that can restore the previous binding, including the absence of a previous value.

Nested scopes make this distinction visible: an inner request identifier must disappear when the inner call returns or raises. Resetting to a guessed default would erase an outer binding. The exercise accepts the variable explicitly, so its ownership and restoration can be tested without depending on logging infrastructure.

```python
from contextvars import ContextVar
request=ContextVar("request",default="none")
token=request.set("outer")
print(request.get())
request.reset(token)
print(request.get())
```

## Review the design

Context tokens preserve nesting and the original binding. They are scoped to their context; passing a token to a different context is an error rather than a portable way to transfer request state.
lessons.task: Implement within_context(variable,value,call) returning call() with the temporary binding. Restore the exact previous context even if call raises.
lessons.starter:
def within_context(variable, value, call):
    return None

checks.name: temporary binding returns a value
checks.code:
from contextvars import ContextVar
v=ContextVar('x',default='none');assert within_context(v,'a',v.get)=='a';assert v.get()=='none'

checks.name: nested context survives inner exit
checks.code:
from contextvars import ContextVar
v=ContextVar('y',default=0)
assert within_context(v,1,lambda:(within_context(v,2,v.get),v.get()))==(2,1)
assert v.get()==0

checks.name: failure restores context

Reset that token in finally instead of setting a default value.

lessons.title: Cancel and await the task you own
lessons.body:
# Cancel and await the task you own

Cancellation is a request delivered at an await point. Calling cancel without awaiting the task leaves cleanup and exceptions unresolved. A parent that owns a task should request cancellation, await completion and suppress only the expected CancelledError.

The coroutine may already have finished successfully or failed before cancellation. Those outcomes must retain their meaning. Catching every exception would hide a broken worker. The tests synchronize through an Event so they verify the actual cleanup path without sleeps that depend on device speed.

```python
import asyncio
async def main():
    task=asyncio.create_task(asyncio.sleep(1))
    task.cancel()
    try: await task
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print("cancelled")
asyncio.run(main())
```

## Review the design

Awaiting establishes the cleanup boundary. A task can refuse cancellation, so production owners also need a shutdown policy for uncooperative work; this contract assumes cooperative coroutines.
lessons.task: Implement async stop_owned(task). Cancel and await it; return None for cancellation or its successful result. Propagate other failures.
lessons.starter:
import asyncio

async def stop_owned(task):
    return None
lessons.solution:
import asyncio
async def stop_owned(task):
    task.cancel()
    try: return await task
    except asyncio.CancelledError: return None

checks.name: awaits cleanup
checks.code:
import asyncio
async def case():
 ready=asyncio.Event();log=[]
 async def work():
  try:ready.set();await asyncio.Event().wait()
  finally:log.append('closed')
 t=asyncio.create_task(work());await ready.wait();assert await stop_owned(t) is None;assert log==['closed']
asyncio.run(case())

checks.name: keeps completed result
checks.code:
import asyncio
async def case():
 async def work():return 7
 t=asyncio.create_task(work());await t;assert await stop_owned(t)==7
asyncio.run(case())

checks.name: does not hide worker failures
checks.code:
import asyncio
async def case():
 async def work():raise ValueError('broken')
 t=asyncio.create_task(work())
 try:await t
 except ValueError:pass
 try:await stop_owned(t)
 except ValueError:return
 assert False,'failure was swallowed'
asyncio.run(case())

hints: Cancellation must be followed by awaiting the task.
Catch asyncio.CancelledError, not Exception or BaseException.
Awaiting establishes the cleanup boundary. A task can refuse cancellation, so production owners also need a shutdown policy for uncooperative work; this contract assumes cooperative coroutines.
lessons.explanation: Awaiting establishes the cleanup boundary. A task can refuse cancellation, so production owners also need a shutdown policy for uncooperative work; this contract assumes cooperative coroutines.

lessons.title: Bound task creation as well as active calls
lessons.body:
# Bound task creation as well as active calls

A semaphore limits active work, but creating one task per input can still exhaust memory before any result finishes. A fixed set of workers with a shared iterator bounds both task count and active calls. Preserve input indices so concurrent completion does not reorder the public result.

TaskGroup gives the workers one failure boundary. If one fails, siblings are cancelled and awaited before control leaves the group. This exercise deliberately accepts a finite iterable and an asynchronous operation; unbounded streams need a separate result-consumption and backpressure contract.

```python
import asyncio
async def main():
    queue=asyncio.Queue(maxsize=1)
    await queue.put("one")
    print(queue.full())
    print(await queue.get())
    queue.task_done()
asyncio.run(main())
```

## Review the design

There is no await between taking an iterator item and assigning it to a worker, so the event loop cannot assign the same item twice. Result storage is still linear in input size; bounded concurrency is not bounded total result memory.
lessons.task: Implement async bounded_map(values,call,limit). Create at most limit worker tasks, preserve result order, reject limit<1, and propagate worker failures through TaskGroup.
lessons.starter:
import asyncio

async def bounded_map(values, call, limit):
    return None
lessons.solution:
import asyncio
async def bounded_map(values,call,limit):
    if limit<1: raise ValueError('positive limit required')
    values=list(values);result=[None]*len(values)
    jobs=iter(enumerate(values))
    async def worker():
        for index,value in jobs:
            result[index]=await call(value)
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as group:
        for _ in range(min(limit,len(values))): group.create_task(worker())
    return result

checks.name: preserves results with bounded activity
checks.code:
import asyncio
async def case():
 active=peak=0
 async def twice(x):
  nonlocal active,peak
  active+=1;peak=max(peak,active);await asyncio.sleep(0);active-=1;return x*2
 assert await bounded_map(range(9),twice,2)==list(range(0,18,2));assert peak==2
asyncio.run(case())

checks.name: empty work and invalid capacity
checks.code:
def _bad(call, error=ValueError):
    try: call()
    except error: return True
    return False
import asyncio
async def f(x):return x
assert asyncio.run(bounded_map([],f,3))==[]
assert _bad(lambda:asyncio.run(bounded_map([],f,0)))

checks.name: failed worker is not a partial success
checks.code:
def _bad(call, error=ValueError):
    try: call()
    except error: return True
    return False
import asyncio
async def bad(x):raise ValueError('bad')
assert _bad(lambda:asyncio.run(bounded_map([1,2],bad,2)),ExceptionGroup)

Create only min(limit,len(values)) workers inside TaskGroup.

lessons.title: Share one in-flight computation per key
lessons.body:
# Share one in-flight computation per key

A cache miss under concurrent traffic can trigger many identical requests. Single-flight coordination shares the in-flight Task for a key. Completed or failed tasks are removed so a later call can retry. This is different from storing a permanent result cache.

One caller cancelling its wait should not automatically cancel work still needed by another caller. Shield protects that shared task from this propagation. The owner still needs a lifetime policy for work that outlives all callers. Tests use Events and checkpoints to measure actual call counts rather than timing guesses.

```python
import asyncio
async def main():
    task=asyncio.create_task(asyncio.sleep(0,7))
    values=await asyncio.gather(task,task)
    print(values)
asyncio.run(main())
```

## Review the design

The identity check prevents an old callback from deleting newer work for the same key. Retrieving a finished task exception prevents an abandoned shared task from producing an unobserved-exception warning.
lessons.task: Implement SingleFlight with async get(key,factory), sharing one running factory(key) task per key. Remove finished tasks, and shield shared work from individual waiter cancellation.

checks.name: coalesces concurrent callers
checks.code:
import asyncio
async def case():
 calls=[];gate=asyncio.Event();s=SingleFlight()
 async def load(k):calls.append(k);await gate.wait();return 8
 a=asyncio.create_task(s.get('x',load));b=asyncio.create_task(s.get('x',load));await asyncio.sleep(0);gate.set()
 assert await asyncio.gather(a,b)==[8,8];assert calls==['x']
asyncio.run(case())

checks.name: cancelled waiter does not cancel the shared task
checks.code:
import asyncio
async def case():

 async def load(k):await gate.wait();return 3
 a=asyncio.create_task(s.get('x',load));b=asyncio.create_task(s.get('x',load));await asyncio.sleep(0);a.cancel()
 try:await a
 except asyncio.CancelledError:pass

asyncio.run(case())

async def case():

 async def bad(k):raise ValueError('x')
 async def good(k):return 4
 try:await s.get('x',bad)
 except ValueError:pass

asyncio.run(case())

Use shield for each waiter and remove only the exact completed task.

lessons.title: Drain a bounded queue before shutdown
lessons.body:
# Drain a bounded queue before shutdown

A queue is not only a container: join tracks unfinished work, and each successful get requires one task_done call. Graceful shutdown stops new production while consumers drain accepted items. Immediate shutdown has a different contract and can abandon queued work.

Python 3.14 provides Queue.shutdown. The local exercise uses its non-immediate mode and verifies that every accepted item finishes before returning. Returning from a producer without joining consumers can report success while writes are still pending. No worker thread or external service is needed to observe this lifecycle.

```python
import asyncio
async def main():
    q=asyncio.Queue()
    await q.put(4)
    q.shutdown()
    print(await q.get())
    q.task_done()
    await q.join()
asyncio.run(main())
```

## Review the design

Graceful shutdown preserves already accepted work. TaskGroup owns the consumer lifetime, and task_done balances each retrieval even if processing later grows an exception path.
lessons.task: Implement async drain(values) with a bounded asyncio.Queue(maxsize=2), one consumer and graceful shutdown. Return processed values doubled in order; call task_done in finally for every received item.
lessons.starter:
import asyncio

async def drain(values):
    return None
lessons.solution:
import asyncio
async def drain(values):
    queue=asyncio.Queue(maxsize=2);result=[]
    async def consume():
        while True:
            try:value=await queue.get()
            except asyncio.QueueShutDown:return
            try:result.append(value*2)
            finally:queue.task_done()
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as group:
        group.create_task(consume())
        for value in values:await queue.put(value)
        queue.shutdown();await queue.join()
    return result

checks.code:
import asyncio
assert asyncio.run(drain([1,2,3,4,5]))==[2,4,6,8,10]

checks.name: empty shutdown completes
checks.code:
import asyncio
assert asyncio.run(drain([]))==[]

checks.name: supports one-pass producers
checks.code:

assert asyncio.run(drain(iter([0,-2,7])))==[0,-4,14]

hints: Run the consumer before filling a bounded queue.
Call shutdown after production, then join inside the TaskGroup.
Graceful shutdown preserves already accepted work. TaskGroup owns the consumer lifetime, and task_done balances each retrieval even if processing later grows an exception path.
lessons.explanation: Graceful shutdown preserves already accepted work. TaskGroup owns the consumer lifetime, and task_done balances each retrieval even if processing later grows an exception path.

lessons.title: Separate failures without flattening away structure
lessons.body:
# Separate failures without flattening away structure

Concurrent operations can fail independently. ExceptionGroup preserves that structure instead of losing all but the first failure. Catching the group as one generic error prevents a caller from distinguishing retryable failures from programming bugs.

A split operation can select one exception type while retaining nested groups and the original leaves. This exercise returns leaf messages for reporting only; it does not pretend that flattening is sufficient for recovery. A recovery policy should continue using subgroup structure and avoid retrying work whose side effects may already have committed.

```python
group=ExceptionGroup("batch",[
    ValueError("bad input"),
    OSError("offline")])
selected,rest=group.split(OSError)
print(type(selected.exceptions[0]).__name__)
print(type(rest.exceptions[0]).__name__)
```

## Review the design

Leaf traversal is useful for diagnostics but should not replace except-star or split when handling failures. Cancellation and interrupts also require separate ownership and propagation policies.

lessons.title: Merge sorted feeds with bounded lookahead
lessons.body:
# Merge sorted feeds with bounded lookahead

A global sort requires every record to be materialized. If each input stream is already sorted, a heap can emit the next smallest record with one lookahead per stream. The memory bound depends on the number of streams instead of the total record count.

Production stream contracts must define ordering and tie behavior. This exercise works with comparable numbers and preserves duplicates. A one-pass test rejects implementations that rewind an input. A prefix test uses an infinite sorted stream, making eager consumption a correctness failure rather than merely a performance concern.

```python
import heapq,itertools
left=iter([1,4,7])
right=iter([2,2,9])
merged=heapq.merge(left,right)
print(list(itertools.islice(merged,4)))
```

## Review the design

The sorted-input precondition is essential. A heap merge cannot repair an internally unsorted source without buffering or reordering it. Output storage is proportional to the requested prefix.
lessons.task: Implement merge_prefix(streams,n), returning at most n sorted values from already sorted iterables. Do not materialize entire streams. Reject negative n.
